newsitem.title: USA: Dallas water department to push for rates rise.
newsitem.headline: Dallas water department to push for rates rise.

text.p: Dallas' water department is proposing a 3.3 percent increase in water rates for the next fiscal year to replace some of the city's old pipelines, department director Terrace Stewart said Thursday.
"Some of these were put in place during World War II and need to be rehabilitated or replaced soon before they become a major expense in the long run," Stewart told Reuters.
He said the increase is also needed to offset a $10 million budgetary gap caused mainly by servicing existing bonded debt.
The Dallas Water Utilities Department current budget is about $301 million and its proposal for the 1997-98 fiscal year, which begins Sept. 1, is about $313 million.

If the City Council approves the rate hike, it would boost the average household's monthly water bill by $1.15 to about $36. The last time the department increased the rate was in 1995 when it went up 3.9 percent.
The issue will come up before the council in August when it considers the city's overall budget.
Some council members have reservations about a water rates rise but Stewart said he expects to win their support.

"The council has always been supportive of our department and I have no doubt that they will do so this time too," Stewart said. "But I can't tell you whether it will be 3.3 percent or less. Right now, all we have done is present an outlook and also our needs."

The water department is a self-supporting enterprise of the city. It does not get any tax dollars and supports itself with revenues from water sales. Capital improvements are funded through bonds, which average about $100 million annually.

Stewart said of the $12 million increase sought in next year's budget, $2.4 million would be available from the existing operating balance. The rest would come from the proposed 3.3 percent rate increase.
